newsitem.title: USA: Florida cuts workers' comp insurance.
newsitem.headline: Florida cuts workers' comp insurance.

text.p: Florida's Insurance Commissioner Friday ordered an 11.2 percent average cut in workers' compensation premiums, a move the department said will save Florida employers $220 million a year.

With the decision, Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson rejected a 0.6 percent increase requested by the National Council on Compensation Insurance Inc, a Boca Raton-based nonprofit group that determines rates for member insurers nationwide. The rate cuts take effect January 1.

"In the end, these savings should be passed on to consumers," Nelson said in a prepared statement. "Along with payroll and rent, insurance is a large part of operating any business, and that includes workers' compensation. Consumers can take heart that we have these costs under control."

Workers compensation rates rose 86 percent during the 1980s and prompted lawmakers in Florida and other states to pass myriad reforms to slow the increase in rate hikes. In 1990, Florida officials ordered a 25 percent rollback in rates after the industry requested a 37 percent boost. Rates were frozen again in 1991.

Nelson said he rejected NCCI's most recent request, which was made in July, because the group failed to take into account savings anticipated as workers' compensation insurance companies begin offering managed care packages.

Under managed care, insurers limit physician access in exchange for lower rates. Managed care was included in a group of reforms passed by Florida lawmakers in 1993 to stop skyrocketing premium increases that many employers said were putting them out of business. Nelson's announcement meant employers would experience premium cuts for the second time in three years. In 1994, premiums were cut 10.6 percent.
Nelson also cautioned said NCCI's plan to switch to a for-profit organization could result in NCCI's inability to act as the sole rate-making organization in Florida.
NCCI can either comply with Nelson's order or appeal his decision through the state Division of Administrative Hearings, a quasi-judicial agency that handles disputes with state agencies.
NCCI officials could not immediately be reached for comment.
